newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau folk sharply eye Hong Kong fate under China.
newsitem.headline: Macau folk sharply eye Hong Kong fate under China.

text.p: Portuguese nationals in Macau have over two years' breathing space before the enclave reverts to China in 1999 but they will sharply scrutinise the impact of Hong Kong's handover to see what it means for Macau.

"We will be looking at Hong Kong to see how it settles down after the handover. As long as people still come here to gamble and to eat, and we can do business, we will stay here," said Afonso Pereira, a Portuguese restaurateur.
Under the Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration of 1987, Macau will revert to China at midnight on December 19, 1999, while Hong Kong returns to China next Monday night.

Macau, a sliver of a territory with just 455,000 people earning most of its income from the casino industry, has been a Portuguese enclave for four and a half centuries, much longer than Hong Kong, which Britain seized 156 years ago.

"Wait for it to settle down. It's just like any company when you change management. It could be better, or it could be just the same. People here care more about food in their stomachs and good jobs than about politics anyway," said Pereira.

The fact that Macau is not a colony as such, but rather a "Chinese territory under Portuguese administration", bodes well for Macau's future, reckons Carlos Ferreira, a Macau-born, 43-year-old civil servant.
"We in Macau think that Macau is a little bit different. We did not confront the Chinese, unlike the British, who seemed to confront the Chinese at every opportunity."
Pereira plans to stay on for at least five years after Macau reverts to China.

"We had three choices -- to go back to Portugal, to retire or to stay here and work. So I decided to learn Mandarin and stay here, otherwise my family and I would have to change our entire lives," he said.
Clara Gomes, a 31-year-old journalist working in the enclave, is confident that Macau will retain its sense of identity after 1999.
"People don't want to see Macau becoming an extension of Zhuhai," she said, referring to the nearby Chinese Special Economic Zone (SEZ).
While younger people in the colony are becoming more political, Gomes said the majority are still mostly interested in ensuring their financial wellbeing after 1999.
Travel agent Filipe Rodrigues, a Eurasian who spent eight years in Canada before returning to take over his family's business, said: "Things should go smoothly."
"We are watching to see what might happen, giving around six months to a year grace period before making any decisions.
"But there shouldn't be any problem with the future," Rodrigues said.
